narrative: The model estimated a 45% chance that you will leave. That is not a certainty, but in this promotion process it is treated as a meaningful retention risk—roughly one chance in two that you may not remain long enough to justify advancement—so the decision is to deny the promotion for now. The strongest factor was that you report no other job opportunities. Among employees predicted to stay, about three-quarters also reported none, so this factor actually pushed your leave risk downward. Your overall experience of one to five years was the second most influential factor and also pushed toward staying; it is common in this group, but shorter tenure still makes a promotion a longer-term bet. The one top factor that pushed toward leaving was how difficult it was for you to get involved in the job—decision-making and having your opinions heard. Only about one in ten employees predicted to stay found this difficult, so this is the clearest warning sign. The organization should explain promotion criteria and discuss a development path with you. You should ask for clearer involvement, feedback and recognition, and explore training or role changes that increase engagement; because you currently see no outside opportunities, this is also a good moment to address whether the role feels stable and worthwhile.
